purpose: Patch Analysis role-capability screening test set (design Sections 17.2/19). Ground truth (mechanism/source/sink/fix) drafted by Claude from direct reading of each case's real diff/source, then CORRECTED after a rigorous user review (2026-10-04) that caught a factual error (CASE-0019), an unverified implementation bug Claude missed (CASE-0022), and several overclaims not supported by the diff alone. Corrections were verified where possible against the real upstream commit message, official GitHub Security Advisory, or a live empirical test -- not re-guessed. Each item's `verification_note` states exactly how its ground truth is grounded.
selection_rationale: 15 pilot cases, stratified across all 4 languages (4 Python, 4 Java, 4 JavaScript, 3 TypeScript) and a diverse set of CWE/vulnerability classes. CASE-0027 was dropped during initial drafting (mechanism genuinely ambiguous from the diff alone) and replaced with CASE-0022 -- which itself needed a correction after review (see below), underscoring why this verification pass mattered.

items.mechanism: The result-extraction protocol trusts subprocess stdout and selects specifically the LAST line starting with a correlation id (`result_line[-1]`), then parses its contents as the execution result -- a permissive matching design that is fragile in principle (vulnerable to result confusion/spoofing if the subprocess's own output could place a coinciding line in that last-matching position). The fix replaces a time-ordered UUID (`uuid.uuid7()`) with a cryptographically random id (`secrets.token_hex(32)`) and hardens the matching protocol to require the id on a specific final line immediately preceding an explicit `__END__` terminator, rather than any line merely starting with the id.
items.source: The sandboxed subprocess's own stdout content -- NOT the correlation id itself, which is generated by this code, not attacker-supplied. The ultimate external entry point (what submits `code_str`/`function_name`/`keywords` to `exec_code`) is not shown in this diff.
items.sink: `result = json.loads(result_line[-1].split(":", 1)[1])` -- parsing the LAST matching line (not the first) and trusting the parsed object as the execution result.
items.fix: Generate the correlation id via `secrets.token_hex(32)` instead of `uuid.uuid7()`; pass it to the subprocess via an environment variable rather than embedding it in generated source; require the second-to-last output line to both equal the expected position AND start with the id, with the true last line required to be the literal `__END__` marker. Note: the final check is still a prefix (`startswith`) test, and passing the id via environment does not by itself prove the executed code cannot read it back.
items.verification_note: Corrected after two rounds of user review. Round 1: removed the overclaim that uuid.uuid7() is practically guessable (RFC 9562 confirms UUIDv7 includes genuine random bits -- not established without more evidence); corrected source (the generated id is not attacker-controlled). Round 2: tightened further -- the parser selects specifically the LAST matching line (`result_line[-1]`), not merely 'any' coinciding line, so the permissive-selection concern is about that specific position, not an arbitrary one. Permissive line-selection behavior is directly observed in the code; an actual exploitable spoofing sequence (a concrete crafted output that would be mis-selected) remains unproven, not demonstrated here.

items.mechanism: Missing privilege check, as the dependency swap implies -- the endpoint required only that the caller be authenticated (any logged-in user), not that they be an administrator. 'Allowing any authenticated user to query the user-listing endpoint' is the apparent implication of this swap, not independently established: neither dependency's implementation nor any other authorization check that might exist elsewhere in the request path is shown in this diff.
items.source: The caller's own authenticated session -- an authorization-logic bug, not a tainted-data-flow bug.
items.sink: NOT FULLY SHOWN -- the `read_users` handler's own return logic (and whether it returns all users or a paginated/filtered subset -- the function signature shows `search`/`role`/`is_active` query parameters, so "full user list" overstates what's confirmed; it's some list of users parameterized by those filters) is not present in this diff hunk, only the dependency line.
items.fix: Change the FastAPI dependency from `deps.get_current_user` (any authenticated user) to `deps.get_current_active_superuser` (admin only).
items.verification_note: Corrected in a second review pass: 'fully verifiable from the diff alone' was too strong -- only the dependency swap is directly shown; the actual return/disclosure logic and whether it's a full or filtered list are not in this diff. 'Unauthorized enumeration of the full user list' softened to avoid asserting more than the visible code shows.

items.mechanism: Potential path traversal: the diff confirms that `uninstall_app` uses the route parameter `app_name` to construct the path passed to `shutil.rmtree()`, with no local containment check shown before deletion. The same class of fix (calling `sanitize_path()` first) is also applied in `install_app` and `lollms_assets`, but what specific filesystem operation each of those two handlers performs on the resulting path is NOT shown in this diff -- those two flows are incomplete evidence, not confirmed in the same way as the uninstall path.
items.source: `app_name`, `asset_type`, `file_name` -- route/path parameters taken directly from the URL.
items.sink: Only `shutil.rmtree(app_path)` (in `uninstall_app`) is a confirmed dangerous filesystem operation visible in this diff. The install and asset-serving handlers' actual filesystem operations (what happens to `REPO_DIR/app_name`, and the asset-serving read) are not shown in this diff hunk.
items.fix: Four calls across three handlers: `sanitize_path(app_name)` in `install_app`, `sanitize_path(app_name)` again (separately) in `uninstall_app`, and both `sanitize_path(asset_type)` and `sanitize_path(file_name)` in `lollms_assets`.
items.verification_note: Corrected in a second review pass: the original said 'three call sites,' undercounting -- there are four calls across three handler functions (`app_name` is sanitized independently in two different handlers). Also restricted the sink claim to the one operation actually confirmed dangerous in this diff (`shutil.rmtree`), since the install/asset-serving operations' exact filesystem calls aren't shown. `sanitize_path()`'s own implementation is still not present in this case's captured source files, so what it actually validates/strips remains unverified.

items.mechanism: Information exposure through an error message -- an EOFError raised while parsing a byte stream (potentially containing sensitive key material) included the raw bytes read so far directly in the exception.
items.source: The relevant source is potentially sensitive stream data (`read_bytes`) already read from the stream being parsed; who or what controls the stream's contents is not established in this diff -- sensitive data and attacker influence are not mutually exclusive categories, so this should not be flatly framed as 'not attacker-controlled' either.
items.sink: `EOFError(read_bytes)` -- the exception's own message/args. Whether this exception ultimately reaches an external-facing log or response is not shown in this diff; that exposure path is assumed context from the CWE-209 classification, not demonstrated here.
items.fix: Replace the raw-bytes-containing exception message with a fixed, generic descriptive string that contains no stream content.
items.verification_note: Corrected per review: reframed source/sink to distinguish 'sensitive data exposed' (this case) from 'attacker-controlled input' (a different vulnerability shape), and flagged that the external exposure path itself isn't shown in this diff.

items.mechanism: This diff adds one class to a denylist `Set` inside Jackson's `SubTypeValidator`. The general mechanism this denylist defends against -- insecure polymorphic deserialization gadget chains, where default-typing deserialization can be made to instantiate attacker-named classes -- is well-established Jackson/CVE context, but is NOT demonstrated by this diff itself (see source/sink).
items.source: NOT SHOWN in this diff, same as the sink -- the claim that an attacker-controlled JSON payload's type-identifying field is what reaches this denylist, and that default typing is enabled in the affected application, is external context from general knowledge of Jackson gadget-chain CVEs, not evidence this specific diff provides.
items.sink: NOT SHOWN in this diff -- this change only adds a class name to a denylist `Set`. The actual vulnerable constructor/setter of `AnterosDBCPDataSource` and the deserialization call site that would invoke it are not present in the captured file.
items.fix: Add the missing gadget class (`br.com.anteros.dbcp.AnterosDBCPDataSource`) to `SubTypeValidator`'s denylist set.
items.verification_note: Corrected in two passes: round 1 marked the sink as not shown; round 2 extended the same caveat to the source/mechanism claims, which are equally external context (general Jackson gadget-chain knowledge) rather than something this diff itself establishes. Only the denylist addition itself is directly verified.

items.mechanism: SQL injection -- a cube name was concatenated directly as a quoted string literal into SQL query text across three separate query-building methods, rather than passed as a bind parameter. (This diff contains substantial unrelated formatting/refactoring noise -- the security-relevant change is specifically these three methods switching to parameterization.)
items.source: `cubeName` -- visibly the value entering the SQL text in this file. Its ultimate external/client-controlled origin (the REST controller) is not shown in this diff.
items.sink: `queryService.querySystemCube(sql).getResults()` -- present in all three removed call sites, executing the string-concatenated SQL.
items.fix: Replace string concatenation (`"= '" + cubeName + "'"`) with a parameterized query -- build a `PrepareSqlRequest` with a bind parameter placeholder (`= ?`) and the value passed separately as a typed `StateParam`, executed via the new `getPrepareQueryResult()` helper calling `queryService.doQueryWithCache(sqlRequest, false).getResults()`.
items.verification_note: Corrected per review: named the exact vulnerable execution call explicitly rather than describing the sink generically, and softened the source description since the REST-layer origin of `cubeName` is not shown in this file.

items.mechanism: This patch (CVE-2024-49771) is the official vendor's acknowledgment that an EARLIER zip-slip fix (CVE-2020-35460, which is what this case's 'vulnerable' version already contains -- a string-based canonical-path prefix check) was itself incomplete: 'there is still a possibility that a malicious path could be constructed which would not be picked up by the original fix' (GitHub Security Advisory GHSA-j945-c44v-97g6). Neither that advisory nor the fixing commit's own message ('Improve the checks for relative traversal. Use java.nio.file.Path for consistent sub-directory checking') discloses the exact bypass string -- an initial draft of this ground truth guessed a specific sibling-directory bypass, but that guess is WRONG: the vulnerable check appends `File.separator` to the prefix, which a careful reader (the user, on review) showed defeats exactly that bypass. The precise exploitable gap in the string-based version is not described in the cited advisory or fixing commit -- a narrower claim than 'not publicly documented' anywhere, which this ground truth does not have the evidence to assert; what's established is only that the maintainer confirmed a gap existed (in those two specific sources) and replaced string comparison with structural `java.nio.file.Path` comparison.
items.source: `entry.getName()` -- the ZIP entry's internal filename, fully controlled by whoever crafted the archive.
items.sink: NOT SHOWN in this diff -- `new File(dir, entry.getName())` constructs a path object and is the subject of the containment check, but the actual file-extraction WRITE operation is not present in this diff hunk.
items.fix: Replace the string-based canonical-path prefix comparison with `file.getCanonicalFile().toPath().startsWith(dir.getCanonicalFile().toPath())`. This literal code change is fully verified; its precise exploit-prevention rationale is not.
items.verification_note: Corrected after the user identified a factual error in the original mechanism (a guessed bypass that doesn't actually work, given `+ File.separator`). Looked up the real upstream source rather than re-guessing: GitHub Security Advisory GHSA-j945-c44v-97g6 (CVE-2024-49771) and the fixing commit (joniles/mpxj@8002802) via `gh api`. The advisory itself does not disclose the exact bypass, so this entry states that honestly instead of inventing a replacement guess.

items.mechanism: The official advisory for CVE-2023-34035 (spring.io/security/cve-2023-34035) describes the vulnerable condition: authorization rules defined via `requestMatchers(String)` can fail to be correctly evaluated against the intended servlet path when an application secures MULTIPLE servlets in the same application (one of them being Spring MVC's DispatcherServlet). This diff's change (from plain-string matchers to MVC-introspection-aware ones) is CONSISTENT WITH that advisory's mitigation, but this diff alone does not show whether this specific sample application actually registers multiple servlets or runs an affected Spring Security version -- those conditions are asserted by the advisory in general, not demonstrated by this file.
items.source: The incoming HTTP request path. Whether it is evaluated under a servlet-mapping configuration the plain-string matcher cannot reliably disambiguate is the advisory's documented CONDITION for the vulnerability to apply, not something this specific diff demonstrates -- same caveat as the mechanism field.
items.sink: The `authorizeHttpRequests` authorization decision -- specifically whether `.permitAll()` or `.authenticated()` is correctly applied to a given request.
items.fix: Replace plain-string `requestMatchers("/login", "/resources/**")` with MVC-introspection-aware matchers (`mvc.pattern(...)`) backed by a `MvcRequestMatcher.Builder`/`HandlerMappingIntrospector`, so the security check resolves the same way Spring MVC's DispatcherServlet does.
items.verification_note: Corrected in two passes: round 1 looked up the official Spring advisory for CVE-2023-34035 and replaced a generic 'MVC mismatch' story with the advisory's actual, narrower condition (multi-servlet applications). Round 2: the diff doesn't show multi-servlet registration or the Spring Security version in use, so the claim was softened from 'this matches the condition' to 'this is consistent with the advisory's mitigation' -- not proof this specific sample meets every documented vulnerability precondition.

items.mechanism: Predictable password-reset token (CWE-640). The official GitHub Security Advisory for this exact CVE (GHSA-98vh-wqw5-p23v, CVE-2022-29174) states that knowing a user's account email/username and stored full name 'increases the chances of guessing' the reset token -- a paraphrase, not a verbatim quote, and weaker than asserting these attributes are 'sufficient' to guess it. The vulnerable version derives the token by hashing these account attributes together with a server-generated timestamp.
items.source: `member.username` and `member.full_name` are account attributes the advisory discusses; the `timestamp` is a SEPARATE, server-generated value (not an account attribute, and not demonstrated to be attacker-controlled or attacker-observable in this diff) that is also an ingredient of the weak token. These are predictable/low-entropy token-generation inputs, not necessarily attacker-controlled fields.
items.sink: Three visible operations: `sha512Hash(member.username + member.full_name, timestamp)` generates the weak token; `db.collection('password_reset').insert(...)` stores it; `countlyMail.sendPasswordResetInfo(member, prid)` sends it to the user. The LATER validation of a presented token against the stored one, and the authorization logic that actually performs the password reset, are not shown in this diff.
items.fix: Generate the token via `crypto.randomBytes(32).toString('hex')` instead of hashing account attributes and a timestamp.
items.verification_note: Corrected in two passes: round 1 cited the official advisory (GHSA-98vh-wqw5-p23v) to confirm the general mechanism. Round 2 found the cited sentence was paraphrased rather than quoted verbatim and overstated as 'sufficient'; corrected to the advisory's actual, weaker claim ('increases the chances of guessing'). Also separated the timestamp (server-generated) from the account attributes (user-associated) in the source description, and expanded the sink to name the three concrete operations actually shown rather than a generic reference to 'the token.'

items.mechanism: Identity-consistency failure after TLS -- a required post-TLS identity re-exchange simply overwrote the established identity with whatever packet arrived next, without verifying it matched the identity established during the earlier (pre-TLS) handshake.
items.source: The post-TLS identity packet received from the remote peer.
items.sink: `this.identity = await this.readPacket();` -- the VULNERABLE assignment, present in both removed blocks in the original code (not the new guarded assignment inside `_exchangeIdentities()`, which is the fix, not the vulnerability).
items.fix: Add `_exchangeIdentities()`, which compares `this.identity.body.protocolVersion`/`this.identity.body.deviceId` (the previously-established identity) against `identity.body.protocolVersion`/`identity.body.deviceId` (the newly-received packet), nulling `this.identity` and throwing on either mismatch. Two distinct defects, both confirmed directly against the diff text: (1) in BOTH branches, `this.identity = null` executes before the thrown error's own template literal references `this.identity.protocolVersion` or `this.identity.body.deviceId` -- since `this.identity` is now null, this throws a TypeError before the intended Error is ever constructed, in both branches. (2) The protocol-version branch's error message additionally has an inconsistent property path for the NEW packet: the comparison correctly uses `identity.body.protocolVersion`, but the message interpolates `identity.protocolVersion` instead -- reading a top-level field rather than the nested one actually being compared. This is a second, independent bug from defect (1); whether it would evaluate to `undefined` at runtime depends on whether `identity` happens to carry an unrelated top-level `protocolVersion` property, which isn't established either way from this diff -- the defect is the wrong property path itself, not a specific claimed runtime value. Neither defect reinstates the original vulnerability (the surrounding catch block still closes the connection either way), but the intended descriptive error message is never actually produced in either branch.
items.verification_note: Corrected across two review passes. Round 1: the sink originally quoted the NEW guarded line, not the actually-vulnerable OLD line -- fixed to point at the removed assignment; also caught the null-then-dereference defect (1) above. Round 2 (independent re-verification): confirmed the exact property paths character-by-character against the diff and found a SECOND defect (2), the inconsistent `identity.protocolVersion` vs `identity.body.protocolVersion` path in the protocol-version branch specifically -- both defects are now stated precisely per-branch rather than described generically.

items.mechanism: Argument injection into a `ripgrep` subprocess -- AT THE CODE LEVEL, search-path and pattern values were appended to the subprocess argument array without a `--` separator, so a value starting with `-` (e.g. ripgrep's `--pre=/bin/sh` preprocessor flag) would be interpreted as a command-line option rather than literal search data, which COULD enable arbitrary command execution IF these parameters are externally reachable with attacker-chosen content and ripgrep's `--pre` (or an equivalent option) is available in the deployed environment -- neither of which this diff demonstrates end-to-end.
items.source: `searchPath` and `pattern` -- parameters this function accepts. Whether and how an external caller can set these to attacker-chosen values is not shown in this diff; call-site reachability is assumed context, not demonstrated here.
items.sink: `spawnSync(rgPath, args, ...)` -- in both call sites (`searchFilesWithRipgrepGlob` and `searchWithRipgrep`), where `args` becomes ripgrep's literal command-line arguments.
items.fix: Insert a `--` separator immediately before the user-controlled positional arguments in both call sites (`args.push("--", searchPath)` and `args.push("--", pattern, searchPath)`), so ripgrep treats everything after it as literal data, not options; additionally reject any `pattern` starting with `-` as defense-in-depth before that push.
items.verification_note: Re-checked the exact `--` placement relative to both `searchPath` and `pattern` directly against the diff per review -- confirmed both call sites place `--` immediately before all user-controlled positional arguments. This confirms the CODE-LEVEL edit; it does not independently establish that these parameters are actually reachable by an external caller, or demonstrate working command execution end-to-end -- those remain plausible but unverified beyond what the diff itself shows.

items.mechanism: Regular-expression denial of service (ReDoS), confirmed via the official advisory for CVE-2018-1109. Structurally: the vulnerable pattern `^\{(,+(?:(\{,+\})*),*|,*(?:(\{,+\})*),+)\}` is an alternation of two branches, each pairing a greedy `,+`/`,*` quantifier with a nested optional group; for an input consisting only of an opening `{` followed by commas and NO closing `}` (the tested input family -- see verification_note for the exact construction), that nested group can only match empty (no literal `{...}` substrings are present to match), but the surrounding comma-quantifier pair can still partition the same run of commas in many ways. Because the input never supplies the required closing `}`, every such partition ultimately fails, forcing the engine to exhaust many partitions via backtracking before reporting failure -- the classic structural shape of a ReDoS-prone pattern. This produced empirically measured super-linear (consistent with roughly quadratic) growth on the tested input family, confirmed across three independent measurement rounds (full detail in verification_note); it is not asserted here to be proven exponential or to hold for every possible input shape.
items.source: The input string being parsed by the `braces` library -- attacker-controlled if the library processes untrusted glob/brace-expression input. (This remains conditional, not demonstrated end-to-end in this diff.)
items.sink: `this.match(/^\{(,+(?:(\{,+\})*),*|,*(?:(\{,+\})*),+)\}/)` -- the exact vulnerable regex literal shown in the diff, invoked via the parser's `.match()` call.
items.fix: The rewrite removes the overlapping/ambiguous repetition structure and eliminates the measured blowup described above FOR THE TESTED INPUT FAMILY. It does NOT preserve the same matching language: a direct counterexample, `{{,}}`, is REJECTED by the old regex but ACCEPTED by the new one (confirmed by executing both patterns against this exact string) -- so this is a behavior change, not a pure performance optimization, and whether the library's overall intended behavior is affected by this language change would need separate, parser-level testing beyond this one regex.
items.verification_note: Corrected across multiple review rounds, now made fully auditable rather than merely asserted. Tested input: `'{' + ',' * n` (an opening brace followed by n commas, no closing brace; `n` counts commas specifically, so total input length is `n + 1` including the opening brace) -- NOT 'comma-only' as an earlier draft said, since the leading `{` is required for the pattern to engage at all. Round 1 ran a live Python timing test, found polynomial/quadratic growth for the old pattern (not exponential, correcting the original claim). Round 2 measurements (Python 3.12.14, 5 measurements, no separate warm-up phase; Node.js 24.19.0, 7 measurements after warm-up -- performed by the reviewing party during that round, not personally re-typed by the human user): old pattern 7.26ms->408.51ms (Python) / 1.74ms->104.31ms (Node) from n=1,000->8,000; new pattern 0.044ms->0.292ms (Python) / 0.0045ms->0.0327ms (Node) over the same range -- and the counterexample `{{,}}` (old: no match, new: match), disproving language-equivalence. A further round, reported by Claude (single-shot, not median-of-several -- environment: Python 3.14.4 / Node.js v24.15.0): `node -e "const old=/^\\{(,+(?:(\\{,+\\})*),*|,*(?:(\\{,+\\})*),+)\\}/; const neu=/^\\{((?:,|\\{,+\\})+)\\}/; for (const n of [1000,2000,4000,8000]) { for (const [name,re] of [['OLD',old],['NEW',neu]]) { const t0=process.hrtime.bigint(); re.test('{'+','.repeat(n)); console.log(n,name,Number(process.hrtime.bigint()-t0)/1e6+'ms'); } }" -- reported output: OLD 1.42ms/5.11ms/16.45ms/46.25ms (n=1,000/2,000/4,000/8,000, ~33x slowdown for 8x input, consistent with the earlier quadratic finding); NEW 0.033ms/0.007ms/0.016ms/0.022ms (non-monotonic at sub-millisecond scale). This non-monotonicity reflects INSUFFICIENT MEASUREMENT PRECISION (a single-shot run at sub-ms scale is dominated by noise) -- it does not favor a constant-time interpretation or any other specific growth-rate claim for the new pattern; no claim about the new pattern's precise growth rate is made here. The old pattern's super-linear blowup and the `{{,}}` counterexample are each reproduced across rounds and need no further re-measurement. The 50K-char/10s figure (security.snyk.io) is noted only as a directional consistency check against the old pattern's measured growth, not as independent validation of any specific timing method.

items.mechanism: Improper host-key verification ordering -- SSH authentication was allowed to proceed and submit credentials before host-key verification had completed, letting a client send credentials to a server whose host key had not yet been confirmed trusted.
items.source: The SSH server's host key -- what `verifyHostKey()` evaluates. `hostVerifiedPromise` itself is an internal synchronization object (not an attacker-controlled entry point); it was mischaracterized as a 'source' in an earlier draft and is now described only as the mechanism gating the real source (the host key) against the sink below.
items.sink: `callback(await this.handleAuth(methodsLeft))` -- submitting authentication credentials to the (possibly unverified) remote host.
items.fix: Add `await hostVerifiedPromise` before proceeding with authentication. The promise's constructor calls `reject(new Error('Host key verification failed'))` when `verifyHostKey()` returns false, and unconditionally calls `resolve()` afterward regardless (not in an `else` branch) -- but this does not reverse the rejection: a Promise's settled state (rejected or resolved) is fixed on first settlement in JavaScript, so once `reject()` has fired, the later `resolve()` call is a no-op. `await`ing this promise therefore does genuinely throw/block on a failed verification, not just on eventual completion.
items.verification_note: This entry's claim is grounded in the promise's constructor (included as an excerpt in the companion review file, not just the diff hunk, since it isn't part of the diff itself). Per review: confirmed the two-callback sequence (`reject(...)` then unconditional `resolve()`) does not undo the rejection, since a JS Promise's settlement is a one-time, first-wins event -- this supports the fix description without independently demonstrating every possible host-verification failure mode or what `handleAuth()` itself returns. Also corrected the source field, which had conflated the synchronization object with the actual untrusted entity being verified (the host key).

items.mechanism: Shell command injection IF the request schema accepts shell-significant characters in these fields (the schema itself is not shown in this diff, so this is conditional, not demonstrated) -- user-controlled values were interpolated into shell command strings executed via `execSync`, which runs through the platform's default shell (not universally `/bin/sh` -- this varies by OS), letting shell metacharacters in those values inject additional commands.
items.source: `parsed.data.tags`, `parsed.data.project`, `parsed.data.identifier` -- tool-call arguments from the MCP client. The schema validation for these fields is not shown in this diff, so whether malicious values would even pass that validation is unverified; the input-building logic for the third (`task add`) call site is also not shown in this diff, only its sink-side change.
items.sink: Three call sites: `execSync(\`task limit: ${task_args.join(" ")} next\`, ...)`, `execSync(\`task ${parsed.data.identifier} done\`, ...)`, and `execSync(\`task add ${task_args.join(" ")}\`, ...)`.
items.fix: Replace `execSync` (shell string) with `execFileSync('task', argsArray, ...)` at all three call sites -- passing arguments as an array directly to the binary, bypassing shell interpretation. This does not establish that every argument is safe under Taskwarrior's OWN command syntax, only that shell metacharacters are no longer interpreted by a shell.
items.verification_note: Corrected across two review rounds: round 1 fixed 'the platform's default shell' instead of asserting `/bin/sh -c` universally, and flagged the schema/`task add`-input-building as outside this diff's visible scope. Round 2 made the mechanism explicitly conditional on the schema accepting shell-significant input, rather than stating the injection as unconditional fact alongside an unrelated caveat about the schema being unverified -- the two should read as one coherent conditional claim, not a claim plus an afterthought.

items.mechanism: OS command injection -- a hostname/IP parameter was used to build a shell command string without validating its contents first, letting a crafted value containing shell metacharacters inject arbitrary commands when executed.
items.source: `host` -- a caller-supplied argument to this function. Its external, attacker-controlled API origin (what ultimately calls `ping(host, ...)`) is not shown in this diff.
items.sink: `cmd = \`ping -w 1 -i 0.2 -c 3 ${host}\`` (and the FreeBSD equivalent) followed by `exec(cmd, (err, stdout) => {...})` -- `host` is interpolated directly into a template-literal shell command string passed to `exec`. This sink is supported by the additional source-file excerpt in the companion review file, NOT present in the diff itself -- the diff only shows the validator being added, not the pre-existing command-construction code it protects.
items.fix: `isValidHost(host)` is called and returns an error via `callback(new Error("Invalid host"))` BEFORE any command construction -- an allowlist-style validator restricting to valid IPv4/IPv6/domain-name characters. For non-ASCII (IDN) hostnames, it checks whether `domainToASCII(host)` would pass the same character check -- but the function does NOT reassign `host` to this converted value. AFTER validation, `host = host.replace("[", "").replace("]", "")` strips the first `[` and first `]` characters (not a global replace) before the command is built -- so `host` is NOT unmodified at the point of use, contrary to an earlier draft of this ground truth; what specifically does NOT happen is substitution of the `domainToASCII()`-converted form. The value that reaches the shell command is the original (possibly non-ASCII) host string with only its first bracket pair stripped.
items.verification_note: Corrected across three review rounds. Round 1 read the full `ping()` function body (beyond the diff hunk) to confirm the sink and validator-gating -- accurate, but not verifiable from the diff excerpt alone that was handed over; the companion review file now includes that excerpt directly. Round 2 caught that `domainToASCII()`'s result is checked but never reassigned to `host`. Round 3 caught that my phrase 'unmodified' was itself a factual error -- `host.replace("[", "").replace("]", "")` DOES run on `host` before the command is built (removing the first `[`/`]`); corrected to describe precisely what is and isn't substituted. Also relabeled the companion file's excerpt as 'abbreviated source excerpt' (it uses `...` and omits implementation detail) rather than 'full ping() function', and softened 'attacker-controlled via whatever API exposes this function' to describe `host` as a caller-supplied argument whose external origin isn't shown.
